steps.body: Multiplying a whole number by 10 makes each digit worth **ten times as much**. In 7 × 10, the 7 ones become 7 tens, or 70. The zero records an empty ones place; no digit is simply moved or glued on.
steps.narration: Multiplying a whole number by 10 makes each digit worth **ten times as much**. In 7 × 10, the 7 ones become 7 tens, or 70. The zero records an empty ones place; no digit is simply moved or glued on.

widget.prompt: A school has 32 classrooms with about 10 kids in each. Slide to estimate the total number of kids.
widget.lowFeedback: Too few — even ONE classroom holds about 10 kids, and there are 32 of them. Slide up.
widget.highFeedback: That's a stadium, not a school! 32 tens land in the hundreds — ease back down.
widget.successFeedback: About 320 — 32 × 10 makes 32 tens, which is 320. Tens make the estimate easy to check.

predict.prompt: 32 classrooms of about 10 kids each — the total lands between…
predict.reveal: 32 × 10 = 320 because every digit becomes worth ten times as much. Thirty-two ones become thirty-two tens, placing the estimate between 100 and 1,000.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents times 5 10.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for times 5 10 must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines times 5 10.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

steps.body: Track how each digit's place value becomes ten times as much.
explanationVariants: 6 × 10 turns each of the 6 ones into a ten: six tens are 60.
Six dimes: each dime is ten pennies, so 6 coins hold 60 pennies.

options.label: Each of the 6 ones becomes a ten — six tens make 60
options.feedback: Exactly: 6 ones become 6 tens, while 0 records the empty ones place.

options.label: Because you can glue a 0 onto any multiplication answer
options.feedback: Gluing zeros only LOOKS like the rule. It happens here because ones become tens — try gluing a 0 for 6 × 5 and it falls apart.

options.label: Because 6 + 10 makes 60
options.feedback: 6 + 10 is 16. Adding joins once; multiplying by 10 turns all six ones into tens.

steps.body: ×5 rides along: **5 is half of 10**, so every ×5 answer is half its ×10 answer — 8 × 10 = 80, so 8 × 5 = 40. That's why ×5 answers always end in **0 or 5**, and why the clock counts by them.

explanationVariants: 6 × 5 is half of 6 × 10: half of 60 is 30.

commonErrors.feedback: 11 adds 6 + 5. Six GROUPS of 5 stack up: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30.
65 glues the digits together. Use the half-of-ten shortcut instead: 6 × 10 = 60, and half of that.
35 is 7 × 5 — one group of 5 too many. Six hops of 5 stop at 30.

steps.body: ×5 answers wear a **uniform** — check the last digit.

widget.prompt: Could each number be a ×5 answer? Sort by its last digit.

items.feedback: 40 ends in 0 — it's 8 × 5. Every ×5 answer ends in 0 or 5.
23 ends in 3. Count by 5s and you only ever land on numbers ending in 5 or 0 — 23 gets skipped.
15 ends in 5 — it's 3 × 5. The 5-count lands right on it.
52 ends in 2, so no ×5 fact reaches it — even though it LOOKS like 5 and 2 swapped places.

widget.missFeedback: Check each number's last digit: 0 or 5 means the 5-count can land there; anything else gets hopped over.
widget.successFeedback: Sorted by uniform! Last digit 0 or 5 — that's the ×5 badge.

explanationVariants: Each clock number is worth 5 minutes: pointing at the 9 means 9 × 5 = 45 minutes.
Count by 5s around the face to the 9: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45.

widget.prompt: The minute hand points straight at the 9. How many minutes past the hour is it?

commonErrors.feedback: 9 is the clock NUMBER, not the minutes. Each number on the face is worth 5 minutes — multiply.
14 adds 9 + 5. The hand has passed NINE marks, each worth 5 minutes: 9 × 5.
95 glues 9 and 5 together — and an hour only has 60 minutes! Nine 5s make 45.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count by 5s once per clock number, stopping at the 9.

steps.body: A smaller stretch of the clock, before recess.
explanationVariants: The minute hand at the 1 means 1×5=5 minutes; at the 4 means 4×5=20 minutes. The gap is 20−5=15.
Turn each clock position into minutes first (5 and 20), then subtract to find the elapsed time (20−5=15).

widget.prompt: The minute hand starts at the 1 (5 minutes past) and moves to the 4 (20 minutes past). How many minutes passed?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 subtracts the clock NUMBERS themselves (4−1) — each number stands for 5 minutes, so convert first: 20−5=15.
25 adds the two times (20+5) instead of finding the gap between them — subtract instead: 20−5=15.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Convert each clock position to minutes first (1→5, 4→20), then subtract to find the elapsed time (20−5=15).

hints: Turn each hand position into minutes first — each clock number is worth 5.
Start: hand at the 3 → 15 minutes past. End: hand at the 9 → 45 minutes past.
Recess runs from 15 to 45 — subtract to find its length.
explanationVariants: Start 3 × 5 = 15, end 9 × 5 = 45; the recess lasts 45 − 15 = 30 minutes.
From the 3 to the 9 the hand crosses 6 numbers, each worth 5 minutes: 6 × 5 = 30.

widget.prompt: Recess starts when the minute hand points at the 3 and ends when it points at the 9. How many minutes long is recess?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 subtracts the clock numbers (9 − 3) — but each number is worth 5 whole minutes. Turn both into minutes first.
60 adds 45 + 15. Recess is the time BETWEEN the readings — find the gap, not the sum.
45 is when recess ENDS. It didn't start at zero, though — it started at 15. Subtract.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Convert both: hand at 3 = 15 minutes, hand at 9 = 45 minutes. The recess is the difference.

takeaways: ×10 makes each digit worth ten times as much; an empty ones place is recorded with 0.
×5 is half of ×10, and its answers always end in 0 or 5.
The clock counts fives: clock number × 5 = minutes.
steps.teaser: your ×2 machine has a turbo button — doubling twice makes ×4, three times makes ×8.

concept.body: Quick rewind. For ×10, every 1 becomes a 10: so 4 × 10 turns 4 ones into 4 **tens** — 40. For ×5, count on your fingers by fives: 5, 10, 15… each finger is one more group of 5.

options.feedback: 15 adds 5 + 10. Multiplying turns all five ones into tens: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.
510 places the digits side by side. Five groups of 10 make five tens, or 50.
